Supplementary Materials 
Shared Flow Fields for Dynamic Navigation in Interactive Strategy Environments 
This document provides implementation procedures, experimental protocols, complete numerical outputs, 
workload matrices, and exploratory summaries supporting the main manuscript. Reference numbers 
correspond to the main reference list. 
Contents: S1 Software and validation; S2 Dynamic planning; S3 Movement; S4 Matched costs and concurrent workloads; S5 
Complete model outputs; S6 Exploratory summaries; S7 Workload matrices; S8 Measurement scopes and numerical checks; S9 
Supplemental acquisition with corrected D* Lite. 
S1 Software and validation 
S1.1 Environment and software provenance 
The project was evaluated with Unity 2022.3.30f1c1. Formal experiments use dedicated research runners 
and generated scenarios; the original project is retained as historical audit material. The movement 
runner uses an existing unit visual prefab with legacy motion components disabled and updates its 
positions from the research movement kernel. 
The research architecture separates a canonical navigation grid, planner interface, dynamic-change 
application, workload runner, metric collector, and bounded structured logger. The navigation layer 
exposes initialization, planning, and change-application operations with explicit versioning. The logging 
layer writes manifests, per-sample results, structural counts, failure categories, and SHA-256 provenance. 
This separation allows the same scenario and workload contract to drive multiple algorithms without 
allowing an algorithm-specific runner to redefine the task. 
The host specification recorded Windows 11 Pro build 26300, an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X3D (16 cores, 32 
logical processors), 33,396,609,024 bytes of RAM, and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4070 Ti SUPER. A 
header audit of all 15,395 retained editor-process logs for the three dynamic-planning studies, SMSB, 
and MQ identifies Unity 2022.3.30f1c1, Windows build 26300, Mono, and editor execution with -
batchmode -nographics (Null Device). Movement and callback lanes instead used standalone-build-
attempt-003, a Mono player launched in batch mode with Direct3D 11. All 1,536 retained player-log 
headers identify driver 32.0.16.1692; the movement design records NVIDIA driver 616.92 and 16,376 
MiB, whereas Unity reports 16,061 MB of VRAM. These are retained as source-specific reports rather 
than treated as interchangeable memory measurements. 
The movement application configured 1920 × 1080 FullScreenWindow mode, quality index 5, vSync 
disabled, no target-frame cap, a 0.02 s fixed step, a top-down orthographic camera, and no UI or debug 
gizmos. These display settings apply to the movement/callback application, not the graphics-disabled 
editor modules. The audit covered 3,552 four-method, 1,600 confirmation, 1,536 expanded-study, 7,843 
SMSB, 864 MQ, and 1,536 movement/callback log headers. All identify Unity 2022.3.30f1c1. Editor 
headers consistently record Windows build 26300 and 31,849 MB physical memory but omit GPU-
driver details; player headers identify the GPU and driver but omit the corresponding OS/RAM fields. 
Hardware-model and display-configuration statements therefore retain their design-record provenance 
rather than implying a complete per-process inventory. 
S1.2 Navigation procedures 
A*-R is stateless between requests and performs a new A* search for each fixed-start plan. D*L owns 
one persistent state instance per agent and repairs that state after changes. C-FF owns one shared multi-
source field and rebuilds the complete field after each relevant change. IDFF owns one shared 
incremental multi-source field and restores consistency only where required before refreshing directions. 
The four implementations use the same directed entry-cost convention, connectivity, and corner-cutting 
rule, while retaining their native state organization.

2 
Algorithms S1 and S2 specify the measured shared-field implementations. Let V denote grid cells, T the 
canonical goal set, and c(u, v) the cost of a legal move: the positive finite traversal cost of v multiplied 
by 1 for an orthogonal move or sqrt(2) for a diagonal move. Each queryable field stores an integration 
value, an owner goal, and a next-cell direction. Relaxation and consistency comparisons use a 1e-12 
tolerance. Equal-cost owners are ordered by (y, x); direction selection further compares remaining cost 
and successor coordinate. C-FF allocates new arrays, revision storage, and a heap at each rebuild, while 
IDFF retains arrays across repairs. Consequently their measured contrast combines update strategy with 
memory-management policy. C-FF and IDFF are study-specific implementation labels. 
Algorithms S1 and S2 map to CorrectedFullRecomputeFlowFieldPlanner.cs (SHA-256 prefix bdaa52bc93950) and 
IncrementalDynamicFlowFieldPlanner.cs (63aa0792bd09), respectively. These source identities are recorded in the SMSB six-
algorithm-fairness-binding.v4_1.json and MQ formal-mq-implementation-manifest.v2_4.json. Algorithm S3 maps to 
Gate14ReMQFormalRunnerV2 and its private-worker executor under the MQ v2 freeze. The historical class name 
CorrectedFullRecomputeFlowFieldPlanner denotes the C-FF implementation throughout this manuscript. Historical movement 
uses the separately frozen standalone build whose Assembly-CSharp.dll has SHA-256 prefix 2f763a06d43a; its identity must be 
preserved when interpreting movement failures. The corrected supplemental builds are documented in Section S9. 
Algorithm S1. Full-Recompute Flow Field (C-FF) 
Input: grid G, canonical goal set T, legal-move relation N(.) 
Output: integration J, owner O, and next-cell direction D 
1   Allocate fresh arrays; set J[v] <- INF, O[v] <- NIL, and D[v] <- NIL for every v in V 
2   Q <- empty deterministic min-heap 
3   for each walkable goal t in T, in canonical order do 
4       J[t] <- 0; O[t] <- t; push the current record for t into Q 
5   while Q is not empty do 
6       u <- pop a record from Q; if stale, continue 
7       for each legal predecessor p of u do 
8           candidate <- c(p, u) + J[u] 
9           if (candidate, O[u]) improves (J[p], O[p]) then 
10              J[p] <- min(J[p], candidate); O[p] <- O[u]; push the revised p into Q 
11  for each walkable, reachable, non-goal cell v do 
12      S <- {s in N(v) : c(v, s) + J[s] equals J[v]} 
13      D[v] <- deterministic minimum of S by (total, owner, remainder, coordinate) 
14      assert O[v] equals O[D[v]] 
15  return (J, O, D) 
On every accepted grid change, build a fresh field by lines 1-15, then replace the old field. 
A plan query follows D until the declared owner goal and requires J to decrease at each step. 
 
Algorithm S2. Incremental Dynamic Flow Field (IDFF) 
Input: updated grid G; change set C; persistent field, Q, revisions, dirty set, cursor 
Output: a queryable field or a resumable PENDING state 
1   For a new change set, mark repair pending and make the field non-queryable 
2   A <- changed cells and their clipped 3 x 3 dependency neighborhoods 
3   for each v in A, mark its direction dirty; UPDATE-VERTEX(v) 
4   while the queue phase is unfinished do 
5       if the budget expired then preserve state and return PENDING 
6       u <- pop the next non-stale inconsistent vertex, if any 
7       if none remains then sort dirty cells, set cursor to 0, and end this phase 
8       else if (rhs[u], rhsOwner[u]) precedes (g[u], gOwner[u]) then 
9           (g[u], gOwner[u]) <- (rhs[u], rhsOwner[u]); invalidate u's queue revision 
10      else (g[u], gOwner[u]) <- (INF, NIL); UPDATE-VERTEX(u) 
11      if u was processed, UPDATE-VERTEX each predecessor 
12      if u was processed, mark its changed direction dependencies dirty 
13  while dirty cells remain from the saved cursor do 
14      if the budget expired then preserve state and return PENDING 
15      v <- next dirty cell; advance cursor; clear D[v] 
16      if v is walkable, reachable, and not a goal then 
17          D[v] <- deterministic successor s with c(v, s) + g[s] equal to g[v] 
18  clear pending and dirty state; expose the field; return COMPLETE 
UPDATE-VERTEX(v): 
19  if v is a walkable goal then (rhs[v], rhsOwner[v]) <- (0, v) 
20  else use the best legal successor via g; blocked/no successor gives (INF, NIL)

3 
Algorithm S2. Incremental Dynamic Flow Field (IDFF) 
21  increment v's revision, invalidating its older queue entries 
22  if g and rhs cost/owner pairs differ, enqueue v with the revised key 
A resume skips lines 1-3 and retains its queue phase and direction cursor. 
A plan call resumes pending repair before following the consistent direction field. 
IDFF initialization sets g and rhs to infinity, clears owners and directions, initializes revision tags and an 
empty queue, and marks every direction dirty. UPDATE-VERTEX seeds each walkable goal with rhs = 
0; the queue is drained and all directions are refreshed before queries are allowed. A queued vertex takes 
the lesser cost/owner pair from g and rhs. The heap orders its stored numeric cost exactly, then owner 
presence (present first), owner coordinate, vertex coordinate, and insertion sequence. Tolerance-based 
consistency checks therefore do not replace the heap's total ordering. Every UPDATE-VERTEX 
increments the vertex revision, invalidating older entries even when the vertex becomes consistent. 
Budget checks occur before queue steps and direction refreshes. Pending repair preserves the queue, 
revision tags, dirty set, and refresh cursor; a resume does not reinitialize the same change set or expose a 
partially repaired field. Each new IDFF repair also allocates two grid-length Boolean scratch arrays, 
scans the affected flags, and clears the grid-length dirty flags. Dirty direction dependencies include the 
changed cell and its geometric predecessors under the connectivity offsets. Bookkeeping includes these 
grid-wide operations alongside local consistency repair. The pseudocode presents the planning 
operations; the implementation additionally validates inputs and records metrics. 
The Expanded Search-Strategy Benchmark adds BiA*-R and LPA* [6, 11]. A*-R and BiA*-R use 
Manhattan distance for four-way grids and octile distance for eight-way grids, scaled by the minimum 
walkable traversal cost. A*-R ends when the goal is removed from its frontier. BiA*-R creates forward 
and reverse frontiers for every request and accepts its best connection when neither valid frontier has an f 
value below that connection cost; reverse expansion uses the original directed edge cost. Neither retains 
search state between requests. LPA* uses backward, goal-rooted g/rhs and queue state per agent with a 
fixed start. D*L instead updates its key offset when the requested start moves. Both persistent per-agent 
implementations update changed cells and their neighborhoods and rebuild their states if a lower 
traversal cost reduces the heuristic scale. The fixed-start studies emphasize update reuse, and D*L and 
LPA* share much of their implemented structure; SMSB consequently records equal deterministic grid 
work and retained state for these two backends. 
The prototype records specification identifiers and hashes, implementation hashes, processed-work units, 
planner instance counts, persistent-state counts, and shared-field counts. These fields prevent results from 
different algorithm identities or state models from being silently combined. 
S1.3 Validation and execution checks 
In the earlier dynamic-planning and movement experiments, a complete Williams block is executed in 
one fresh Unity process. Each eligible algorithm appears at most once in that process, each sample 
reconstructs and disposes mutable state, and the process exits after the block. Algorithms are paired 
within a block, while blocks or campaign-level summaries supply the independent units specified by 
each analysis. Four-algorithm blocks use an even-order Williams design; two-algorithm blocks use 
balanced AB/BA order. SMSB instead assigns each of the six matched algorithm lanes to its own fresh 
Unity process, as described in Section S4.1. 
Preflight and post-run checks verify scenario hashes, algorithm identities, schedule position, predecessor 
balance, state reset, grid/planner version agreement, result-file hashes, process identity, memory 
conditions, and completion receipts. Partial blocks retain their failure category. Missing, zero, non-finite, 
failed, and over-budget observations are recorded with reason codes. 
Correctness checks cover route legality, shortest-path or field-reference agreement, deterministic identity, 
event order, and structural agreement with the archived reference cases. A separate array-scan shortest-
path reference checks C-FF integration values and owners, followed by legal-direction construction; its

The Four-Method Dynamic-Update Benchmark included all 3,552 completed eligible block processes 
and 10,176 algorithm samples. Each of P1–P4 had 10,176 eligible continuous observations, P5 had 
10,176 eligible count records, and no continuous metric was missing. The shared queue contained 1,536 
processes; the two heterogeneous queues contained 1,008 processes each and formed 1,008 balanced 
matched superblocks. 
The Expanded Search-Strategy Benchmark completed 1,536 of 1,536 planned blocks and 6,144 samples 
with no whole-block replacements. The Independent Flow-Field Confirmation completed 1,600 paired 
blocks and 3,200 samples under its fixed 32-campaign, 50-block-per-campaign design. The Movement 
and Scaling Benchmark accepted 1,536 complete blocks and 6,144 algorithm-lane samples, with each 
experiment's formal raw tree held read-only during analysis. 
SMSB accepted 1,296 matched superblocks and 7,776 algorithm lanes. The 7,843 trusted natural process 
exits comprise 7,776 measurement processes, one instrument self-test, 54 oracle batches, and 12 empty-
boundary checks. All correctness and D1–D4 measurement-validity gates passed. Two technical failures

S2 Dynamic planning protocols and complete telemetry 
S2.1 Task definitions and measurements 
The Four-Method Dynamic-Update Benchmark scenario bundle contains 53 byte-canonical scenarios 
and 74 campaign profiles. The matrix covers core conditions and sampled grid-size, agent-count, 
dynamic-footprint, reachability, and goal-count levels. Every scenario materializes its grid, walkability, 
traversal costs, connectivity, starts, goals, scheduled changes, operation budgets, and deterministic 
identity. Regeneration and load-time validation check the complete structure and hashes. Section S7 
specifies every matrix family, seed rule, and cohort mapping. 
Three goal cohorts are retained separately. The shared-goal cohort has one destination and includes A*-R, 
D*L, C-FF, and IDFF. Both heterogeneous cohorts submit each agent's declared destination. A*-R and 
D*L search for that destination. C-FF and IDFF construct one multi-source field from the complete goal 
set, but accept a request only when its destination equals the least-cost reachable owner at the start under 
the stated tie rule. A different owner causes InvalidRequest; the runner does not retarget the request or 
restrict the field to an agent-specific goal subset. Consequently the grouped-field cohort measures a 
mixture of accepted and rejected assigned-goal requests.

5 
The early dynamic-planning endpoints use planner-reported operation telemetry. For each tick containing 
scheduled changes, the runner applies all changes in order and then queries every agent from its fixed 
scenario start. A dynamic phase is the sum of the recorded planner repair timings and subsequent plan 
timings for that tick. A*-R includes change acknowledgement and fresh searches; D*L includes its per-
agent updates and queries; C-FF includes full field rebuilding and queries; IDFF includes incremental 
repair, direction refresh, any plan-triggered completion, and queries. One counted repair is the backend 
change-application call, which can update several per-agent state instances. Initialization and the initial 
pre-event queries are recorded separately. 
P1 is the sum of dynamic-phase times divided by the number of scheduled change events. A same-tick 
group contributes its elapsed time once but contributes every event to the denominator; P1 is normalized 
handling time per scheduled event, not the mean time per distinct event tick. P2 is the nearest-rank P95 
of the m phase times within a sample, using ordered value ceil(0.95m). For the four-phase schedules in 
the early matrix, this statistic is the sample maximum. P3 sums reported initialization, initial-plan, and 
later plan/repair times and divides by agent count. Its initialization boundary differs by implementation: 
IDFF creates its persistent arrays and queue before the stopwatch, while C-FF allocates during the timed 
rebuild. P3 retains these implementation-specific initialization boundaries. Positive P1–P4 sample 
endpoints are summarized by geometric means. P5 reports exact plan and repair overrun counts for the 
10,000-ms per-operation termination budget; initialization has a separate 30,000-ms budget. These are 
termination budgets. 
P4 is the recorded dynamic memory diagnostic divided by scheduled-event count. The implementation 
uses the nonnegative difference in GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread readings when either reading 
is positive; otherwise it uses the clipped increase in GC.GetTotalMemory(false). The fallback measures 
heap-occupancy change, whereas the first branch measures a cumulative counter difference. The 
archived output contains the resulting diagnostic but not the branch or both snapshots; successful queries 
can report zero despite creating path objects. P4 is retained with this counter-dependent interpretation 
and cannot establish comparable cumulative allocation savings across implementations. SMSB D3 is 
defined independently by its event-window instrument. 
The Movement and Scaling Benchmark adds movement traces, latched arrival state, completion 
categories, critical movement violations, and main-loop callback intervals. Its movement and callback 
measurements use separate lanes; neither is treated as a planning-timing sample. Section S3.3 specifies 
the M4 timing boundary. 
S2.2 Four method study 
The Four-Method Dynamic-Update Benchmark used the complete 74-campaign matrix: 32 shared-goal 
campaigns, 21 per-agent heterogeneous-goal campaigns, and 21 grouped-field heterogeneous-goal 
campaigns. Every campaign contained 48 complete Williams blocks. The shared cohort therefore 
contributed 1,536 block processes and 6,144 algorithm samples; each heterogeneous cohort contributed 
1,008 block processes and 2,016 samples. In total, 3,552 eligible fresh-process blocks and 10,176 
samples were completed, with 2,544 samples per algorithm. 
The heterogeneous cohorts form 1,008 matched superblocks with the same scenario, repetition ordinal, 
and deterministic input identity. Process order is balanced: 504 run the per-agent cohort first and 504 the 
grouped-field cohort first. The secondary comparisons retain these cohort identities, but grouped-field 
timings include owner-mismatch rejection and cannot establish equal successful routing service. 
P1 was the sole confirmatory endpoint. Five shared-goal contrasts formed one family: C-FF/A*-R, C-
FF/D*L, IDFF/A*-R, IDFF/D*L, and IDFF/C-FF. Lower P1 is better, so a ratio below one favors the 
numerator. D*L/A*-R was diagnostic rather than part of the confirmatory family. P2–P5 and all 
heterogeneous comparisons were supportive or secondary.

6 
Each block contributed a paired natural-log ratio. The 48 block ratios were averaged within each shared 
campaign, and the 32 equally weighted campaign means supplied the matrix estimate and standard error 
(their sample standard deviation divided by sqrt(32)). The frozen analysis used a normal approximation: 
the four field-versus-search contrasts were directional, with lower ratios favored, and IDFF/C-FF was 
two-sided. Holm adjustment [30] covered those five p values. Ordinary 95% intervals were two-sided. 
Five Bonferroni intervals with 99% individual coverage provide at least 95% family-wise coverage. The 
campaign means supply the inferential units. P5 is reported as exact overrun counts and operation 
denominators. 
P3 reported operation cost and the agent-count scaling model address different summaries. The latter 
uses the specified shared-goal agent-scale family and its level-dependent seed rule (Table S15). 
Heterogeneous analyses average 48 matched superblocks within each of 21 equally weighted scenario 
pairs. The five specified contrasts use 99% individual Bonferroni intervals; the additional D*L/A*-R 
interval is diagnostic. 
S2.3 Expanded search study 
The expanded study acquired new measurements of BiA*-R, LPA*, C-FF, and IDFF on the 32 shared-
goal scenarios. Each campaign contained 48 four-algorithm Williams blocks, giving 1,536 fresh 
processes and 6,144 algorithm samples. All planned blocks completed with zero whole-block 
replacements. 
The primary family contained BiA*-R/C-FF, BiA*-R/IDFF, LPA*/C-FF, and LPA*/IDFF. P1 retained 
the same definition and lower-is-better direction. Each campaign averaged its 48 paired block log ratios. 
The 32 campaign means then entered two-sided one-sample t inference with 31 degrees of freedom and 
standard error equal to their sample standard deviation divided by sqrt(32). The analysis reported raw P1 
geometric means, ordinary 95% intervals, Holm-adjusted p values across four contrasts, and Bonferroni 
intervals with 98.75% individual and at least 95% family-wise coverage. This t procedure differs from 
the normal approximation used in the earlier four-method study. The four P1 contrasts define the study's 
comparison family. 
S2.4 Repeat run field confirmation 
The repeat-run field confirmation acquired new observations for IDFF versus C-FF P1 across the fixed 
32 shared-goal campaigns. Each campaign contains 50 paired blocks, balanced as 25 in each execution 
order, for 1,600 fresh processes and 3,200 samples. Its separate raw-data identifiers distinguish this 
acquisition from the earlier measurements. 
The single prespecified contrast was d = ln(P1_IDFF/P1_C-FF). The primary estimator equally weighted 
the 64 campaign-by-order strata, each containing 25 independent blocks. A Welch–Satterthwaite 
variance approximation produced a two-sided 95% interval and p value at alpha = 0.05. Because the 
confirmatory family contained only one contrast, no multiplicity correction was applied. The protocol 
treats missing or structurally invalid planned blocks as a non-estimable confirmation result. Unlike the 
earlier 32-campaign-mean analysis, whose uncertainty includes between-campaign variation, this 
estimator treats campaign and order strata as fixed and propagates the repeat-block variance within them. 
The resulting interval quantifies repeat-run precision for the specified matrix. 
The confirmation execution contract bound the analysis-plan SHA-256 before the new acquisition: it was 
frozen at 03:36:25 UTC on 11 October 2026, and the launch receipt was issued at 03:55:15 UTC that day. 
This establishes specification before this confirmation acquisition, after the earlier study had motivated 
the comparison. Recalculation from 1,600 hash-verified paired workload records reproduces the log ratio 
-0.2293235621, standard error 0.0042822829, and Welch–Satterthwaite degrees of freedom 337.6492334. 
It does not establish that all analyses in the paper preceded all earlier observations.

S2.5 Complete endpoint summaries

Across the 1,008 heterogeneous samples per algorithm, each backend received 430,080 queries,

S3 Historical movement protocol and decision rules 
S3.1 Design and event schedule 
The historical Movement and Scaling Benchmark independently evaluated A*-R, D*L, C-FF, and IDFF. 
This module has its own observations and analysis. Its main module comprised eight frozen shared-goal 
conditions, C01–C08, at N = 128. The selected conditions varied grid size (64 × 64 or 128 × 128), four- 
or eight-neighbor connectivity, weighted or uniform costs, obstacle proportion (0.25 or 0.10), and 
dynamic footprint (9 or 81 cells). These eight selected conditions cover those factors; Table S16 maps 
every condition to its source scenario and factors. The corrected supplemental main-condition acquisition 
is reported separately in Section S9. 
Each design cell contained B = 48 complete blocks, with each of the four Williams rows used 12 times. 
A block ran all four algorithms on restored copies of the same frozen input in one fresh Unity process. 
The main module comprised eight conditions, two measurement lanes, and 48 blocks, yielding 768 
processes. The quantity module used C01 and C07 as anchors at N = 1, 8, 32, 128, and 512; N = 128 
reused the corresponding main-module observations once, and the remaining levels added 768 processes. 
The full design therefore contained 1,536 complete blocks and 6,144 algorithm-lane samples. 
For N below 128, starts were canonical prefixes of the source scenario's ordered starts. For N = 512, the 
original 128 starts were retained and 384 additional distinct, initially walkable and goal-reachable cells 
were selected by a deterministic SHA-256 ordering. Map, goal, event, and algorithm semantics were 
unchanged across quantity levels. 
The movement experiment schedules five changes in a maximum 180 s simulated window: block one 
footprint and unblock a disjoint footprint at tick 10 (0.20 s), in orders 0 and 1, increase traversal costs at 
30 s, decrease them at 90 s, and restore the initial state at 150 s. The synchronizer applies both tick-10 
changes before advancing agents. The unblock operation does not undo the newly blocked footprint, 
which remains blocked during the subsequent short trajectories. All 2,592 successful movement runs 
across the main and quantity conditions finish by 11.84 s and retain exactly those two initial events. 
Their completion results therefore cover the resulting obstacle configuration but not the later cost 
changes.

At each event, the same NavigationChangeSet was applied to the canonical grid and the active planner. 
Grid, planner, and rendered-world revisions had to agree, and the structural log recorded event identity, 
tick, order, changed-cell count, old and new grid versions, planner repair status, and world revision. 
Missing, duplicated, reordered, or content-drifted events failed the block. An algorithm that completed 
before a later event retained its completion result and was not reactivated to force equal event exposure. 
S3.2 Arrival and movement validity 
A unit was considered arrived when its grid cell equalled the shared goal cell and its horizontal distance 
from the cell center did not exceed 0.75 cell size for ten consecutive 0.02 s fixed ticks. Arrival was 
latched. After arrival, the runner retains the latched state. 
M1 was simulated elapsed time from measurement release until every registered unit latched arrival, 
calculated as the final tick count multiplied by the 0.02 s fixed step. It did not include wall-clock waiting 
caused by planner computation. Lower is better. A run that did not complete retained the failure-coded 
value M1 = 180 s and its terminal category; this value is not an observed successful travel time. M2 was 
the mean cumulative horizontal distance to first latched arrival over a common four-algorithm unit mask.

S4.2 Managed private workload execution 
The managed multi-query module evaluates concurrent execution of independent private workloads for 
C-FF and IDFF. Each individual field build, repair, and query remains serial, while the worker executor 
distributes whole workloads. 
Each of 36 complete matched blocks reused its own 16 private workload lanes across all 24 fresh Unity 
processes (two algorithms × 12 conditions), yielding 864 serial processes and 13,824 lane executions. 
The lane composition varied between blocks. Inputs came from a frozen pool of 108 workloads, three per 
SMSB structural cell; across the 576 block-lane assignments, each of the 36 cells appeared 16 times. 
Each lane owned a private grid and planner, assignment followed lane ordinal modulo worker count, and 
outputs were restored in ascending lane order. Every query was checked against a cached algorithm-
neutral oracle after the timed batch. Section S7 records the input binding and workload envelope. 
The 12 conditions comprised two ST-direct serial controls, managed W1, W2, W4, and W8 under each 
of the prespecified large-L3 and high-frequency single-CCD placements, and balanced dual-CCD W8 
and W16. The latter allocated four or eight workers per CCD. ST-direct used the caller thread; the 
confirmatory worker-scaling tests used the managed conditions. Windows CPU-set binding was 
mandatory, one logical sibling was used per physical core, and no measured Unity processes ran 
concurrently. The endpoint was complete-batch wall time in seconds, with lower values preferred.

Within each single-CCD policy, a block supplied the equal-weight ordinary-least-squares slope of 
log(batch wall time) on log2(worker count); exponentiation gives the wall-time ratio per worker doubling. 
The dual-CCD estimand was the within-block W16/W8 log ratio. The complete matched block, rather

The MQ code adds a fixed-worker executor and a measured workload wrapper around the C-FF and
